extracted.intended_audience: journalism students and reporters (news writers, broadcast reporters)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for when and how to attribute information in news stories for print, web, and broadcast, covering direct and indirect attribution, paraphrase, anonymous sourcing, sourcing agreements, and quote mechanics. Geared to reporters deciding what to attribute and how to present sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute nearly all information
rubrics_metrics.description: Nearly all information in a news report should be attributed, either directly or indirectly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The only major exception is information gathered by a reporter who is an eyewitness to an event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect attribution for short items / generic official source
rubrics_metrics.description: In a short news item, the attribution may be to a generic official source (e.g., 'The highway was closed for two hours, police said').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there is more information that came directly from the same official source, you don’t have to keep repeating 'police said … police said' if it’s already clear who the main source is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use paraphrase when a direct quote is unnecessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Convey information that comes directly from a source by paraphrasing rather than quoting when a direct quote isn't needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The accident took place on a sharp curve during a thunder storm, state police Sgt. James Millbrook said.' Paraphrase is appropriate for factual or explanatory material that doesn't require the source's exact words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcast attribution: lead with source and use actualities
rubrics_metrics.description: In radio or television the attribution usually comes first, and reporters use actualities (short video or audio clips of the source) instead of long direct quotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good: 'Police said the accident was a result of poor road conditions.' Not OK: 'Police said the accident was a result of quote – poor road conditions — unquote.' Best practice: identify speaker before clip (e.g., 'Sgt. Jenny Malone explains how the accident occurred.') and include clip metadata/outcue (e.g., '[CLIP #1 MALONE – OUTCUE: “…do our best under the circumstances.”]'). Avoid 'scare quotes' in broadcast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use direct quotes for color, explanation, and emotional force — not for basic facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct quotes should be used to add color, explain viewpoints, convey emotional drama, or let sources speak directly about issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use direct quotes for basic factual material (e.g., statistics or mundane facts). Choose quotes that best represent the source’s opinion or point of view. Example of good quote vs. bad quote provided in text to illustrate the difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct structure and mechanics for direct quotes in print/web
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotes should follow standard punctuation and attribution structure: opening quote marks, capitalize first word, end the quoted sentence with a comma inside the quotes, close quote marks, then attributional verb and the name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use full name and title on first reference and only last name on subsequent references (vary with appropriate pronoun use). Example structure provided in text. Follow print/web conventions for punctuation and attribution placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use neutral attributional verbs
rubrics_metrics.description: Attributional verbs in news articles should be neutral in tone or implication (e.g., 'said' is the usual neutral choice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid biased verbs that imply falsehood ('claimed'), imply truth ('pointed out'), imply undignified behavior ('screamed'), or imply a courtroom context ('testified'), unless those characterizations are factually accurate. Reporters need not worry about repeating 'said' through a story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymous attribution only when necessary to protect sources or minimize harm
rubrics_metrics.description: It may be appropriate to keep the name of a source confidential when shielding sources during an investigation or protecting victims/witnesses to minimize harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anonymous attribution should never be used to cover up lazy reporting. Example of improper anonymous use: quoting an identified, non-vulnerable student as 'one student said' when there is no reason to protect identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: On the record is the default
rubrics_metrics.description: On the record means everything is on the record; direct quotes can be attributed to a fully identified source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the normal status for public hearings and statements made to the media by public figures or officials. Only rare agreements alter this.

rubrics_metrics.name: On background: limited attribution with editorial oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: On background is used when officials brief the press in a non-official way; the information can be reported but the source is described in generic terms (e.g., 'a high-level State Department official').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors will insist on knowing who the source is and why the source must stay on background. Use on background when private context needs confidentiality but reporting the information is still important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chatham House Rule: report viewpoints without direct attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: In meetings following Chatham House Rule you may report information and points of view but without direct attribution to named individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common in the UK and Europe for political meetings; treat like an 'on background' arrangement for attribution purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deep background: extreme anonymity used rarely and with editorial justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Deep background attribution attributes information only to vague labels like 'a source' or 'a government source' and is used in very rare circumstances (e.g., national security).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors will typically insist on knowing the identity and reasons for deep-background status; use only when absolutely necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Off the record means information will not be used
rubrics_metrics.description: Off the record is a promise that the information will not be used by the reporter, even if it is later confirmed by other sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not agree to go off the record lightly. There's usually no reason to go off the record with public figures; for private people unfamiliar with media, prefer 'on background' to protect identity while allowing reporting. Off-the-record promises should be rare and made only with full understanding of consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine factual information can be paraphrased or shown visually
rubrics_metrics.description: Routine information that is factual or descriptive can be paraphrased rather than quoted and may be better displayed in an easy-to-understand map or infographic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use paraphrase or visual presentation for routine data to avoid cluttering copy with unnecessary direct quotes.
